scores.evidence: The title asks one precise question (how a draft is claimed so a double click can't send it twice). The subtitle names the audience (new engineers) and the scope.
There are three runtime boxes at the same level (browser, app server, Postgres), each inside its deployment zone. Code-level detail stays in the notes.

The diagram is tightly focused and the omissions are listed in the footer. However, the race it exists to explain (two concurrent requests where one gets 'none') is only described in text, never drawn, and the 'skipped' reply path back to the browser is not shown.
Both arrows are numbered, labelled, marked sync, and the key covers responses. With only two edges the ordering is trivial, and the concurrent second click isn't shown as its own event.

Frames separate the owner device, Vercel (hosted, managed) and Postgres (hosted, provider not verified). Each frame wraps a single node, so they add little beyond the labels. The trust boundary (owner-only auth) isn't shown.

Flow runs clearly left to right with no crossings, and text is readable at 1194x834. Arrow labels are small and sit over the frame borders. About 40% of the canvas is empty top and bottom while the notes are dense.

The key explains frames, boxes, the cylinder, arrow direction including the response, and sync. Flow type is also written on each arrow, so meaning doesn't depend on colour alone. Names match the code (sendAction, sendMessage, messages).

The notes cover the important failure modes: suppression rather than exactly-once, guards resetting the row to failed or skipped, rows stuck in 'sending' after a crash, the 3h health check for LinkedIn only, and no recovery for email. None of this appears on the drawing itself.

Dated 2026-11-04 at revision f467a33 with local edits. The owner is shown as Unassigned and live runtime is marked NOT verified. The claims match lib/engine.ts:1346-1358. The cap of 3 applies because production was not verified.
A newcomer can explain the claim mechanism from the notes, but has to picture the race between two clicks without a drawing of it. The 'skipped' message is never shown returning to the UI.

coldRead: The owner clicks Send in the Today view or a conversation view in their browser. The browser calls the sendAction server action on the Next.js app server hosted on Vercel, passing the message id and any edits. sendMessage then runs a single atomic UPDATE…RETURNING against the messages table in Postgres. That statement only matches outbound rows whose status is draft or failed. It sets status to 'sending' and saves any edits in the same step. If no row comes back, a second click or another tab has already claimed the draft, so the request returns 'skipped: Already sent or no longer a draft.' This prevents duplicate sends but does not guarantee delivery. Later guards can reset the row to failed or skipped. If the process crashes after the claim, the row stays stuck in 'sending' and can't be claimed again. The health check flags only LinkedIn rows stuck for more than 3h, and nothing recovers email rows automatically. Delivery, drafting, cron jobs and the worker are out of scope.
inaccuracies: Atomic claim note: the claim UPDATE in lib/engine.ts:1348-1354 also clears error and sets sentAt and updatedAt, which the note omits. This matters because a failed retry clears its previous error.

The Postgres cylinder says 'draft/failed → sending' but leaves out that the guards in lib/engine.ts:1360-1364 later move the row back to failed or skipped with sentAt set to null. The node suggests a one-way transition.

The app server node attributes the claim to sendMessage via sendAction (app/(app)/actions.ts:363). That is correct, but sendMessage calls loadSettings() before the claim (engine.ts:1344), so the claim is not the first database call. This is minor.
improvements: Draw the race: show two concurrent Send requests (click 1 and click 2) hitting the same row, with one getting the row back and the other getting 'none → skipped'. That makes the core idea visual instead of text-only.

Add the response or outcome back to the browser ('skipped: Already sent…' versus continuing to the guards) and a small status-transition strip: draft/failed → sending → sent | failed | skipped | stuck.

Use the empty vertical space: put the frames and notes closer together, and keep arrow labels off the frame borders. Mark the crash-after-claim risk on the server→Postgres edge itself, not only in a note.
